title: Given the root of a binary tree, return its level order traversal, meaning the node values grouped level by level from top to bottom, left to right within each level.
shortTitle: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal: BFS with queue
keyPoints: Use a FIFO queue and snapshot its size at the start of each level to process exactly one level per outer iteration.
Enqueue the root, then loop: dequeue levelSize nodes, collect their values, and enqueue their non-null children.
The size snapshot is what separates levels; without it you cannot tell where one level ends and the next begins.
Time is O(n) because each node is enqueued and dequeued once; space is O(w) where w is the maximum tree width.
This base pattern powers zigzag traversal, right-side view, per-level averages, and many BFS variants.
Prefer ArrayDeque over LinkedList for the queue because of better cache locality and no node-allocation overhead.

s1_definition.oneliner: Use a queue and snapshot its size at each step to process exactly one full level before moving down.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Level Order Traversal** – visits a binary tree breadth-first, one level at a time, from top to bottom and left to right within each level.
- **Queue-based BFS** – enqueue the root, then repeatedly dequeue all nodes at the current level, collect their values, and enqueue their children.
- **Size snapshot** – at the start of each level, record `queue.size()` and process exactly that many nodes to cleanly separate levels.
- **Complexity** – O(n) time; space proportional to the maximum width of the tree.
- **Variants** – zigzag order, right-side view, per-level averages, and per-level max all build on this base pattern.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants to read the National Bank of India org chart rank by rank: first the branch manager alone, then all direct reports together, then all of their reports together. He keeps a line of people to visit. He notes how many are in the line right now, processes exactly that many as one rank, and as he does he adds each person's reports to the back of the line for the next rank.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Level Order Traversal
  ─────────────────────

  Tree:        1
             /   \
            2     3
           / \     \
          4   5     6

  Queue walk:
  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Start: queue = [1]                        │
  │                                           │
  │ Level 0: size=1, process [1]              │
  │   enqueue children: [2, 3]                │
  │   output: [1]                             │
  │                                           │
  │ Level 1: size=2, process [2, 3]           │
  │   enqueue children: [4, 5, 6]             │
  │   output: [2, 3]                          │
  │                                           │
  │ Level 2: size=3, process [4, 5, 6]        │
  │   no children                             │
  │   output: [4, 5, 6]                       │
  │                                           │
  │ Queue empty → done                        │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Result: [[1], [2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Level order traversal is breadth-first: I visit every node at the same depth before moving deeper, using a FIFO queue. The single technique that separates levels cleanly is snapshotting `queue.size()` at the start of each outer iteration and dequeuing exactly that many nodes. While processing, I enqueue their children, which belong to the next level and wait in the queue until the current level is done.

The time complexity is O(n) because every node is enqueued and dequeued once. The space is proportional to the maximum width of the tree, since the queue at its fullest holds one entire level. For a balanced tree that can be roughly n/2 nodes, but for a skewed tree it is just 1.

This base pattern is the foundation for nearly every level-aware BFS variant. Zigzag order reverses alternate levels. Right-side view collects only the last node per level. Per-level averages sum and divide. All of them reuse the same size-snapshot loop and differ only in what they collect from each level.

In my project at the National Bank of India, I used this to produce a rank-by-rank view of the loan approval hierarchy, so compliance reviewers see all approvers at the same authority level grouped together. The left-to-right order within each rank encodes seniority, and the queue-based traversal with a fixed count per level keeps both grouping and ordering correct.

Remember one sentence: snapshot the queue size at each level, dequeue exactly that many nodes, and enqueue their children for the next level.
